paragraphs: Both Susan B. Anthony and Frederick Douglass argue that America has failed to uphold its founding promises of freedom and equality, but Douglass develops this idea more effectively because of his powerful emotional appeals and sharp exposure of national hypocrisy. In her speech, Anthony relies on a logical and legal approach, quoting the Declaration of Independence and asking, "how can 'the consent of the governed' be given, if the right to vote be denied." This question effectively highlights the constitutional contradiction of barring women from voting, clearly demonstrating that the government is withholding natural rights. However, Douglass creates a far more compelling argument by contrasting America's celebrated ideals with the brutal reality of slavery, passionately declaring to his white audience that "your shouts of liberty and equality, hollow mockery." Rather than simply debating the law, Douglass uses vivid, scathing imagery of violence and oppression to prove that the nation's celebration of freedom is an active "sham" for millions of enslaved people. While Anthony's reasoned legal argument is logically sound, Douglass is ultimately more effective because his intense rhetoric forces listeners to confront the deep moral shame of America's broken promises.

Although her legal points about the Constitution is very logical. Frederick Douglass develop the idea that America is breaking its founding promises way more effectively because his words makes you feel the horror of slavery. Douglass tells the crowd that 'your shouts of liberty and equality, hollow mockery' to prove that the country is living a lie, he uses passionate anger instead of quiet legal reasoning. Because Douglass shows the bloody reality of what the nation is doing, he convince the audience far better than Anthony that America has completely betrayed its ideals.

Both Susan B. Anthony and Frederick Douglass argue that America fails to keep its original promises, but they approach the issue from very different angles. The central idea of Anthony's whole speech is simply that she committed a crime by casting a ballot in the presidential election. She relies heavily on foundational texts to support her claim, pointing out that the Declaration of Independence guarantees unalienable rights and asking, "for, how can 'the consent of the governed' be given, if the right to vote be denied." In contrast, Douglass confronts the nation's severe hypocrisy during a national celebration, describing how "your shouts of liberty and equality, hollow mockery" prove that the Fourth of July only highlights the oppression of enslaved people. Between both speakers, Douglass develops the idea the most effectively because his passionate imagery and harsh tone make the nation's moral failure feel undeniable and urgent, while Anthony focuses more on a technical legal breakdown.

Susan B. Anthony was arrested for voting in an election and Frederick Douglass gave a speech on the fourth of July. In On Women's Right to Vote, she quotes the Declaration of Independence to argue that governments derive their just powers from the "consent of the governed." She points out women cannot give consent without the ballot it proves America is breaking its founding promises. Frederick Douglass talks about how bad slavery is to his crowd because they are celebrating freedom while millions of people are still enslaved. He says to the slave the holiday is "a thin veil to cover up crimes which would disgrace a nation of savages." Which makes the listeners feel guilty about their country's awful hypocrisy. Overall Douglass develops the idea more effectively than Anthony because his angry tone really exposes the cruelty of the nation, so high schools need to make every student read both texts.

Although Susan B. Anthony and Frederick Douglass both show that America failed to keep its founding promises, Douglass develops this central idea far more effectively because his words create a much stronger emotional impact. Anthony relies strictly on legal documents to prove women deserve the ballot, quoting the Declaration of Independence where it says, "All men are created equal, and endowed by their Creator with certain unalienable rights." She argues that having unalienable rights means rights cannot be alien or foreign to anyone, which shows the government broke its word by being mean to women citizens. On the other hand, Douglass challenges the audience more powerfully when he tells them that "to him, your celebration is a sham; your boasted liberty, an unholy license." By calling liberty an unholy license, Douglass means that white Americans got an official legal permit from church leaders to do wicked deeds without punishment. He also states that "there is not a nation on the earth guilty of practices more shocking and bloody," which proves that America has too much blood on it, so the nation broke every promise it made in the past. Furthermore, Douglass says the nation's Fourth of July sermons are "mere bombast," showing that politicians drop verbal bombs on listeners to frighten people away from truth. Douglass is just way more effective. While Anthony makes a logical case using founding texts, Douglass is more persuasive because his vivid imagery exposes the harsh reality of how hypocritical the country really is when celebrating freedom while keeping humans in bondage.

Both Susan B. Anthony and Frederick Douglass argue that America is failing to live up to its founding ideals, but Douglass develops this idea more effectively because of his powerful emotional appeals and urgent moral tone. In her speech, Anthony builds a clear and logical legal argument using the Declaration of Independence, pointing out that governments are meant to secure natural rights rather than grant them. She directly exposes the nation's political hypocrisy by asking, "for, how can 'the consent of the governed' be given, if the right to vote be denied," effectively using the founders' own words to defend her right to vote as a citizen. However, Douglass creates a much stronger impact by moving beyond legal debates to expose the deep moral failure of the entire country. He refuses to calmly argue whether enslaved people deserve freedom, explaining that the nation needs "not the gentle shower, but thunder" to wake its conscience. He powerfully tells his audience that to an enslaved person, "your shouts of liberty and equality, hollow mockery; your prayers and hymns, your sermons and thanksgivings, with all your religious parade and solemnity, are to him mere bombast, fraud, deception, impiety, and hypocrisy." While Anthony's logical breakdown of constitutional principles is convincing, Douglass is ultimately more effective because his vivid imagery and fiery passion force the audience to confront the horrific human suffering and absolute contradiction between American celebrations of liberty and the brutal reality of slavery.

Anthony makes some general points about government rules, which basically shows that America has had a lot of issues with its laws over the course of history. In contrast, Douglass delivers a much more devastating critique of America's betrayal by asking his audience, "What to the American slave is your Fourth of July?" and directly labeling the country's celebrated freedom as a "hollow mockery" while millions remain in chains. He backs up this accusation with visceral details of enslaved people being beaten with sticks and torn from their families, which forces listeners to confront how cruel slavery is compared to the founding ideals citizens are cheering for. Ultimately, Douglass is more effective than Anthony because his fiery tone and vivid evidence make the nation's hypocrisy feel undeniable and urgent, whereas Anthony's speech reads like a legal debate that lacks the same emotional and moral power.
